defects.claim: Capping the governor wait at 250 ms fixes the livelock without introducing a new failure mode.
defects.scenario: BackgroundWorkGovernor.whenClear (libs/backend/vscode-core/src/diagnostics/background-work-governor.ts:281-327) resolves 'timeout' after maxDeferMs with no re-check of state, and waitForGovernor treats a resolved (non-thrown) outcome as success and calls hardStop(), which does not re-read the governor either. The governor's own 'lagging' state exists specifically to stop background work from running while the main-thread event loop is already measured slow (TASK_2026_481/context.md: 54 lag warnings, worst block 2,912.9 ms, worst single SQLite statement 1,672.7 ms on this exact host, all on the one shared better-sqlite3 connection). Retention's own delete-batch comment (memory-retention-config.ts:58-62) documents 133-1730 ms for a 200-row batch on a comparably sized file. With governorMaxDeferMs cut from the governor's built-in 10-minute starvation ceiling to 250 ms (RETENTION_GOVERNOR_MAX_DEFER_MS, memory-retention-config.ts:93-100), a run that starts while state='lagging' or 'foreground-busy' will time out on essentially every one of its ~100 per-run waitForGovernor calls (50,000-row cap at ~500 rows/batch) and proceed to execute a synchronous purge/quarantine/delete batch anyway. If that batch lands anywhere near the worst-case durations already measured on this host (1672-1730 ms), the main thread freezes for that long on top of the pre-existing lag — repeated up to ~100 times in one run. The fix trades a 60-second zero-progress livelock for periodic multi-hundred-millisecond-to-1.7-second main-thread stalls scattered across every hourly retention run, which is precisely the freeze class BackgroundWorkGovernor (and its 'lagging' state in particular) was built to prevent.

defects.claim: The existing 50,000-row limits let the 171,524-row backlog drain over four successful runs.
defects.scenario: The only spec exercising a busy governor mid-run ('a governor timeout leaves budget for a batch instead of consuming the run') sets `governor.clear = true` immediately after releasing the first waiter, so every subsequent waitForGovernor call in that same run takes the isClear() fast path and never waits or times out again — it proves one deferred batch can still complete, not that ~100 consecutive 250 ms-capped waits under sustained lag/foreground pressure still fit 50,000 rows of real batch work inside the 60 s wall budget. No test (unit or integration) runs a full-scale 50,000-row/60,000 ms scenario with a governor that stays busy across the whole run and with batch durations in the 120-1730 ms range the codebase's own comments document for this file size. The 'four runs' figure is correct arithmetic (ceil(171524/50000)=4) only if every run reaches its full 50,000-row cap; under the load profile actually measured on this host (TASK_2026_481: 71 slow SQLite statements totalling 23.2 s, worst 1,672.7 ms, all on the shared main-thread connection retention also uses), a run could spend a large share of its 60 s budget on slow batches and 250 ms waits and fall well short of 50,000 rows, so the backlog could take substantially more than four hourly runs to drain.

testsRan: Running target test for project @ptah-extension/memory-curator (N=1, confirmed via run-many, not positional nx test): Test Suites: 42 passed, 42 total; Tests: 706 passed, 706 total; Time: 34.146s. Matches the implementer's reported 42/706. The new/changed assertions in retention-run-budget.spec.ts and memory-retention.service.spec.ts were inspected and do pin the new behaviour (they assert the OLD buggy outcomes — e.g. report.status 'partial'/purgeCalls 0 — are now replaced by 'completed'/purgeCalls 1, and the old it.each expecting maxDeferMs===remaining budget was replaced with a fixed-ceiling assertion), so these are not tests that would pass unchanged against the pre-fix code.
mentorNote: Cutting the governor's deferral ceiling to 250 ms removes the livelock, but 'timeout' in BackgroundWorkGovernor is not a status check — it means 'stop waiting and run anyway,' regardless of whether the governor is idle-busy (foreground) or genuinely mid-freeze ('lagging', the state this exact class exists to protect). On a 1.2 GB file where single statements already measure up to 1.67 s on the shared main-thread connection, a 250 ms cap all but guarantees retention batches execute during the freeze instead of after it. The ceiling needs to distinguish 'foreground busy, safe to nudge in' from 'event loop already lagging, do not add work,' or retention needs to move its writes off the main thread (which TASK_2026_481 is already scoping) rather than just shrinking how long it waits before barging in.
